paragraphs: Min-max optimization involves two players pushing the same objective in opposite directions. This paper studies a particular version in which the maximizing player must make greedy updates until reaching a first-order stationary point. The minimizing player chooses update directions using a proposal distribution, which also helps define what counts as an equilibrium.

For a smooth, bounded objective that need be neither convex nor concave, the authors prove convergence to their approximate local equilibrium. The result assumes access to a proposal distribution for the minimizing player and stochastic gradients for the maximizing player. Its iteration bound does not depend on dimension. However, the equilibrium reached depends on the proposal distribution, so the guarantee concerns a specific, distribution-dependent solution concept.

The authors test the algorithm on difficult mathematical objectives and GAN training losses. For GANs, they propose directions using stochastic gradients. The reported experiments show convergence on the test functions and stable GAN training without mode collapse on the evaluated synthetic and real-world datasets.
icml-2022-a-convergent-and-dimension-ind.tldr: A min-max algorithm has a dimension-independent iteration guarantee for a proposal-dependent local equilibrium and shows stable GAN training in experiments.

paragraphs: Accelerated gradient methods can reduce the number of optimization steps needed in ordinary Euclidean spaces. This paper extends that idea to Riemannian optimization, where the space has a curved geometry. It considers geodesically convex objectives and the stronger geodesically strongly convex case, adapting the acceleration principle associated with Nesterov's method.

The proposed algorithms are computationally tractable first-order methods, meaning their updates use gradient information. Under the standard assumptions invoked in the paper, their iteration complexities match those of Nesterov acceleration in Euclidean spaces for both objective classes. The authors describe their scheme as the first fully accelerated method for geodesically convex optimization, qualified by their knowledge of prior work.

The analysis introduces results controlling metric distortion and carefully constructed potential functions to track progress. It also connects the discrete algorithms to previously studied continuous-time acceleration dynamics as the step size approaches zero. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results. Together, these contributions address both how to implement acceleration on curved spaces and how to justify its convergence.
icml-2022-accelerated-gradient-methods-f.tldr: Tractable accelerated methods match Euclidean Nesterov iteration complexities for geodesically convex and strongly convex optimization under standard assumptions.

paragraphs: Curriculum reinforcement learning trains an agent through a sequence of tasks that starts easier and becomes more demanding. Such sequences can help solve complex tasks, but deciding how to generate a useful curriculum remains a separate challenge. This paper studies how to automate that choice for a learning environment.

The authors build on the idea of expressing a curriculum as an interpolation between distributions over tasks. In this view, curriculum generation changes which tasks the learner is likely to encounter as training progresses. After identifying issues with existing approaches, they formulate this movement between task distributions as a constrained optimal transport problem. This gives the construction of the curriculum an explicit optimization formulation.

Benchmark results show that the resulting curricula can improve on existing curriculum reinforcement learning methods across tasks with different characteristics. The finding supports constrained transport as a useful way to organize learning experiences. The reported benefit is empirical: the approach achieves high performance in the evaluated settings, rather than establishing that every environment benefits from the same curriculum construction.
icml-2022-curriculum-reinforcement-learn.tldr: Formulating curriculum generation as constrained transport between task distributions improves reinforcement learning performance in varied benchmarks.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation aims to replace a large training collection with a compact synthetic dataset that retains useful training information. This paper addresses a limitation of existing approaches: under a small storage budget, the way synthetic examples are represented can restrict what they express and make their optimization difficult.

The authors introduce a parameterization that takes regularities in data into account and generates multiple synthetic examples within a limited storage budget. The central idea is to improve how that budget represents training information. They also analyze shortcomings of gradient matching methods for condensation and develop an optimization technique intended to transfer training information into the synthetic dataset more effectively.

These representation and optimization changes are combined into one algorithm. The authors report substantial improvements in condensed-data quality over the state of the art on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and Speech Commands. The results support treating the representation of synthetic data and its optimization as connected design choices, with both contributing to more effective condensation.
icml-2022-dataset-condensation-via-effic.tldr: A data-aware synthetic representation and improved optimization produce higher-quality condensed datasets within a limited storage budget.

paragraphs: Group convolutional networks incorporate geometric structure into their architecture, helping them use parameters efficiently and improve accuracy. This paper examines the representations these networks learn and finds considerable redundancy in their convolution kernels. That observation motivates sharing more weights across parts of the transformation group.

The authors construct kernels that separate subgroup and channel dimensions, allowing additional weight sharing. They also provide a continuous parameterization for separable kernels to obtain equivariance to arbitrary affine Lie groups. Equivariance means the representation changes consistently with the geometric transformations built into the model. The approach therefore targets computational redundancy while retaining an explicit relationship to those transformations.

Across several vision datasets, the proposed sharing improves performance and computational efficiency. In many tested settings, separable networks outperform their non-separable counterparts with only a fraction of the training time. The efficiency gain also enables networks equivariant to planar scaling, rotation, and translation together. This additional structure improves every evaluated task and achieves state-of-the-art results on rotated MNIST.
icml-2022-exploiting-redundancy-separabl.tldr: Separable group convolutions reduce redundant parameters and computation while improving performance across the evaluated vision tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often needs many observations, making it attractive to collect experience with multiple agents. Sending all that experience to a central location can be expensive and expose local behavior policies. This paper considers agents that instead maintain local model copies and collaborate on a global model without sharing their individual data or policies.

The authors develop federated versions of on-policy temporal-difference learning, off-policy temporal-difference learning, and Q-learning. Their analysis includes multiple local updates and Markovian sampling, where observations arise from a dependent sequence. This matters because collecting N times as much data with N agents does not by itself establish that learning converges N times faster.

For all three algorithms, the authors prove a convergence speedup linear in the number of agents within their analyzed framework. They obtain a unified proof by expressing the algorithms as instances of federated stochastic approximation with Markovian noise. The contribution connects distributed data collection to a convergence guarantee while explicitly accounting for dependence in the sampled experience.
icml-2022-federated-reinforcement-learni.tldr: Federated TD and Q-learning achieve provable linear speedup with agent count in an analysis that includes Markovian sampling and multiple local updates.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization evaluates the worst loss in a small neighborhood around the current model parameters. This encourages solutions with flatter surrounding loss, associated with better generalization and robustness. The paper questions how that neighborhood is defined: ordinary SAM uses a Euclidean ball, although neural networks often represent probability distributions.

Fisher SAM replaces that ball with an ellipsoid determined by Fisher information. This makes the neighborhood reflect the statistical geometry of the model's parameter space. The motivation is that a seemingly small or large parameter displacement need not correspond to the same degree of change in the underlying distribution. Ignoring that geometry can make SAM probe points at inappropriate distances.

The authors also caution that adapting neighborhood shape using parameter magnitudes can potentially distort its structure severely. Their proposed alternative ties the shape to information geometry instead. Experiments on several benchmark datasets and tasks demonstrate improved performance for Fisher SAM, supporting the practical value of changing how the sharpness neighborhood is measured.
icml-2022-fisher-sam-information-geometr.tldr: Fisher SAM uses information-geometric neighborhoods to measure sharpness and improves performance on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: A learned model of a physical system may struggle when a new system follows similar general dynamics under different physical conditions. This paper addresses that transfer problem with context-informed dynamics adaptation, or CoDA. It aims to adapt efficiently using only a few observations from the new environment.

CoDA learns across multiple environments, each with its own dynamics and contextual parameters. A hypernetwork conditions the dynamics model on a context vector, with both learned jointly from observations. The formulation constrains the space of candidate models during adaptation. This restriction is intended to make it easier to find suitable dynamics from limited data while sharing useful structure across environments.

The authors provide a theoretical motivation and report state-of-the-art generalization on a collection of nonlinear dynamical systems spanning different application domains. On those systems, they also show that physical system parameters can be inferred from the learned context vectors with minimal supervision. Thus, the context representation supports both adaptation and extraction of information about the system.
icml-2022-generalizing-to-new-physical-s.tldr: CoDA uses learned environment contexts to adapt dynamics models to new physical systems from few observations.

paragraphs: Many adversarial-example detectors rely on statistical differences between natural inputs and deliberately perturbed inputs. Evaluating those defenses requires attackers that actively try to evade detection. This paper addresses the difficulty of constructing such adaptive attacks, which can otherwise leave detector evaluations incomplete.

The proposed statistical indistinguishability attack, SIA, optimizes an objective intended to make adversarial examples match natural inputs in the distributions of their neural-network representations. It targets every network layer simultaneously. The authors show why that matters: examples that appear indistinguishable at one layer may still look different at another, leaving a detector with a usable signal.

SIA is formulated for detectors that inspect a collection of adversarial examples together. The authors also find it effective against four detectors of individual adversarial examples, two dataset-shift detectors, and one out-of-distribution detector from published work. These results suggest that distribution matching can provide a useful adaptive test across several detector types, strengthening security evaluation beyond attacks that ignore the detector.
icml-2022-generating-distributional-adve.tldr: SIA crafts adversarial inputs whose representations resemble natural data across network layers, providing an adaptive test for statistical detectors.

paragraphs: Guided-TTS addresses speech synthesis when recordings of the target speaker have no transcripts. Its approach separates learning how that speaker's speech sounds from guiding the generated speech toward the requested content. This allows the target speaker's untranscribed audio to support a text-to-speech system.

The system combines an unconditional diffusion model with a separately trained phoneme classifier. The diffusion model learns to generate speech from untranscribed recordings without conditioning on text. During synthesis, the phoneme classifier guides generation toward the desired speech content. That classifier is trained on a large speech-recognition dataset, so the absence of target-speaker transcripts does not mean the entire system avoids transcribed training resources.

The authors introduce norm-based scaling to reduce pronunciation errors arising from classifier guidance. They report performance comparable to Grad-TTS on LJSpeech without using its transcripts for the target speaker. Further experiments show good performance across diverse datasets, including long-form untranscribed speech. The findings support separating speech generation and linguistic guidance when target-speaker transcription is unavailable.
icml-2022-guided-tts-a-diffusion-model-f.tldr: Guided-TTS combines diffusion speech generation with phoneme-classifier guidance to synthesize speech without target-speaker transcripts.

paragraphs: Learning fair representations aims to construct features that satisfy fairness goals concerning sensitive variables such as gender or race. Adversarial training is a common approach, but the discriminator used to assess the representation is often chosen heuristically. This paper proposes a more explicitly justified discriminator choice.

The method uses an integral probability metric with a particular parametric family of discriminators. Its central theoretical contribution relates fairness of the learned representation to fairness of a prediction model that uses that representation as input. This connection matters because the eventual decision comes from the downstream predictor, so assessing only the intermediate features does not directly establish the relevant prediction-level result.

Numerical experiments show that the proposed method is computationally lighter and more stable than comparison approaches using more complex discriminators. Its final prediction models are competitive with or superior to those alternatives in the reported experiments. The paper therefore combines a theoretical link between two levels of fairness with evidence that a simpler adversarial component can remain practically effective.
icml-2022-learning-fair-representation-w.tldr: A structured discriminator family links representation fairness to prediction fairness while yielding lighter, more stable adversarial training in experiments.

paragraphs: Switching dynamical systems describe time series whose evolution changes between different modes. For systems that evolve continuously, the paper considers switching stochastic differential equations controlled by a Markov jump process. This combines continuous evolution with changes in the governing dynamics, but makes inference computationally difficult.

The authors propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm built as a Gibbs sampler. They state that it efficiently produces samples from the exact continuous-time posterior processes. The target is the distribution of possible underlying processes given observations, so the method provides a way to represent uncertainty about the system's evolution and switching behavior within this model formulation.

The framework also supports Bayesian estimation of model parameters. In particular, it estimates the diffusion covariance, a quantity often held fixed in stochastic differential equation models. The authors evaluate the approach under the modeling assumption and compare it with an existing variational inference method. The stated contribution is an inference framework with an exact continuous-time posterior target and broader parameter estimation.
icml-2022-markov-chain-monte-carlo-for-c.tldr: A Gibbs sampler enables inference for continuous-time switching systems and Bayesian estimation that includes diffusion covariance.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes difficult when clients have different kinds or amounts of data. Their local networks can develop inconsistent representations, making the shared global model converge unstably. This paper introduces an architectural regularization method intended to keep local learning more compatible with the global model.

The method adds auxiliary branches to each local network by joining local and global subnetworks at several levels. These branches form hybrid pathways that combine the two sources of model structure. Online knowledge distillation then trains representations in the main local pathway to agree with those in the auxiliary pathways. Using several joining levels lets this alignment act at different depths of the model.

The authors report that the technique strengthens the global model even when client data are not identically distributed. It can be applied across various federated learning frameworks without extra communication costs. Their empirical studies show gains in both accuracy and efficiency over existing methods, supporting architectural alignment as a practical response to heterogeneous client data.
icml-2022-multi-level-branched-regulariz.tldr: Hybrid local-global network branches improve federated learning under client heterogeneity without adding communication costs.

paragraphs: Recording many neurons across brain regions creates an opportunity to connect detailed neural activity with observable behavior. It also creates a modeling challenge: sensory signals, neural events, and actions operate at different scales. This paper aims to model their dependencies together, where predominant approaches use relatively separate techniques for those scales.

The authors propose an end-to-end model based on flexible, computationally tractable neural-network point processes. The framework characterizes relationships among stimuli, actions, and neural data within a shared model. Its purpose is to connect the microscopic activity captured in neural recordings to the larger-scale processes associated with behavior, making those relationships accessible to joint analysis.

The model is applied to public Neuropixel recordings from mice performing a visually guided task. It is also tested on synthetic data from interacting sensory and integration circuits modeling motion discrimination. The authors report better performance than previous approaches and new insights into neural activity's relationship with behavior. These findings support joint modeling across the two evaluated data settings.
icml-2022-neural-network-poisson-models-.tldr: An end-to-end neural point-process model jointly captures stimulus, neural-activity, and behavior dependencies, outperforming prior approaches in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers learning to a target domain without target labels. The paper begins with a fundamental obstacle: without additional assumptions, the target relationship between features and labels cannot generally be identified. It addresses this ambiguity by assuming that causal mechanisms change minimally across domains.

The authors encode that idea in a latent-variable model with two parts. One contains components whose distributions remain unchanged across domains; the other contains a sparse set of changing components. They further restrict how domain shift influences the changing part. Under conditions described as mild, they prove partial identifiability of the latent variables, which in turn establishes identifiability of the target data-label distribution.

The practical framework, iMSDA, follows these theoretical insights. Experiments show that it outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods on benchmark datasets. The approach matters because it explicitly models limited change alongside invariant structure. Its identification result depends on the stated structural assumptions, while the experiments provide evidence for the resulting method in the evaluated adaptation settings.
icml-2022-partial-disentanglement-for-do.tldr: iMSDA models invariant and sparsely changing latent factors to support target-domain identification under assumptions and improve adaptation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds representations using positive and negative sample pairs. Those comparisons also determine which examples become neighbors in the learned feature space. This paper examines that connection through neighborhood component analysis, offering a stochastic nearest-neighbor interpretation of contrastive learning.

The interpretation becomes a basis for designing new training losses. Rather than treating pairwise comparisons only as isolated attractions and separations, the framework relates them to neighborhood information in the representation. The authors propose a series of losses that outperform existing ones and develop an integrated loss-design methodology intended to support both accuracy and robustness on downstream tasks.

With the integrated framework, the authors report improvements of up to 6% in standard accuracy and 17% in robust accuracy. These are the reported upper ends of the improvements, rather than gains promised for every task. The contribution is both conceptual and practical: a neighborhood-based account of contrastive learning leads to concrete objective functions with experimentally improved downstream performance.
icml-2022-revisiting-contrastive-learnin.tldr: A stochastic nearest-neighbor view of contrastive learning guides new losses that improve standard and robust downstream accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential choice among infinitely many options whose expected rewards deteriorate whenever they are selected. The deterioration can follow an arbitrary trend, subject to a maximum rate ρ that is o(1). The learner must decide when an option remains worthwhile and when to abandon it.

The authors establish a worst-case regret lower bound of order max{ρ^(1/3)T, √T}, where T is the number of rounds. When the maximum deterioration rate is known, their algorithm matches this bound up to polylogarithmic factors. It combines an upper-confidence-bound index for each option with a threshold that determines whether to keep selecting it or remove it from consideration.

When the rate is unknown, the authors adapt both the confidence index and the threshold. This gives a regret upper bound of order max{ρ^(1/3)T, T^(3/4)}, again with polylogarithmic factors suppressed. The results distinguish the guarantees available with and without knowledge of deterioration, while showing how confidence-based selection can be combined with explicit abandonment decisions.
icml-2022-rotting-infinitely-many-armed-.tldr: Confidence-based selection and abandonment thresholds achieve near-optimal regret for infinitely many deteriorating options when the maximum deterioration rate is known.

paragraphs: Saliency methods explain image predictions by highlighting pixels they regard as important to the model. Evaluating those explanations is difficult because researchers usually lack a known account of the model's actual predictive reasoning. Without that reference, judging whether a highlighted region accurately explains a prediction becomes a separate unresolved problem.

The paper introduces SMERF, a synthetic benchmarking framework that makes ground-truth reasoning available for evaluation. It also lets researchers control the complexity of that reasoning. These two capabilities allow saliency methods to be assessed against a defined reference while varying how demanding the explanation problem is. The framework therefore targets the evaluation obstacle directly.

Experiments with SMERF reveal significant limitations in existing saliency methods. The stated finding concerns their performance in this controlled framework, where explanations can be compared with known reasoning. The authors present SMERF as a useful tool for developing new methods because it supplies an explicit target for evaluation and a way to adjust the complexity of the task.
icml-2022-sanity-simulations-for-salienc.tldr: SMERF evaluates saliency explanations against known reasoning in synthetic settings and exposes significant limitations in existing methods.

paragraphs: This paper implements neural-network training within secure multi-party computation, using quantization suited to that setting. The work addresses whether training performed entirely through secure computation can achieve accuracy close to ordinary plaintext training. It combines complete network implementations with new protocols for mathematical operations needed by the training process.

For MNIST, the authors train a network with two convolutional and two dense layers to 99.2% accuracy in 3.5 hours, reaching 99% in under an hour. They report an accuracy gap within 0.2 percent of the same network trained in plaintext and claim the first entirely MPC-trained MNIST classifier to reach that proximity. They also implement AlexNet for CIFAR-10, which converges within a few hours.

The protocol contributions cover exponentiation and inverse square root. Experiments include up to ten parties across honest-majority and dishonest-majority settings, with both semi-honest and malicious security. This range connects the training demonstration to multiple MPC security models, while the reported timings and accuracies establish concrete feasibility for the evaluated networks.
icml-2022-secure-quantized-training-for-.tldr: Quantized secure multi-party training achieves near-plaintext MNIST accuracy and supports neural-network training across several MPC security models.

paragraphs: In online learning with graph feedback, the graph determines which outcomes become observable after an action. Algorithms specialized for stochastic or adversarial environments can perform poorly when the assumed environment is wrong. This paper seeks one algorithm with strong guarantees in both settings without requiring that prior choice.

The work handles general feedback graphs, extending beyond earlier assumptions of undirected edges and self-loops at every vertex. Without a self-loop, selecting an action may not reveal even that action's outcome. This makes exploration more costly and complicates the balance between gathering information and choosing actions that currently appear useful.

The proposed algorithm uses a carefully designed exploration-exploitation trade-off. The authors prove regret growing polynomially in log T in the stochastic setting and minimax-optimal regret of order T^(2/3), with logarithmic and horizon-independent factors suppressed, in the adversarial setting. They describe this as the first such best-of-both-worlds result for general feedback graphs, to their knowledge. The guarantee accommodates both environments within the same algorithm.
icml-2022-simultaneously-learning-stocha.tldr: One algorithm achieves strong stochastic and minimax-optimal adversarial regret guarantees with general graph feedback.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images, but previous empirical results suggest a tension between density estimation and sample generation performance. This paper investigates that relationship by examining which diffusion times contribute most to each goal. Its empirical evidence attributes much of density estimation to small diffusion times and sample generation to large ones.

Training a score network accurately across the whole time range is difficult because loss scales differ substantially across diffusion times. The authors introduce Soft Truncation to address this training problem. It replaces a fixed truncation hyperparameter with a random variable, changing a static training choice into a randomized one. The technique is presented as broadly applicable to diffusion models.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10, CelebA, CelebA-HQ at 256 by 256 resolution, and STL-10. The contribution links those results to an empirical account of why different diffusion-time regions matter for different objectives. It motivates adjusting the training procedure to accommodate that imbalance when learning scores across the full time range.
icml-2022-soft-truncation-a-universal-tr.tldr: Soft Truncation randomizes a diffusion-training cutoff to address imbalanced loss scales and achieves strong image-generation benchmark results.

paragraphs: Clinical datasets often contain many unlabeled examples but few labels because expert annotation takes substantial effort. Active learning can reduce that burden by selecting informative examples. This paper addresses two connected decisions: which examples to acquire and whether each selected example should actually be sent to an expert.

For acquisition, Bayesian Active Learning by Consistency, or BALC, perturbs both the input instance and the network parameters. It measures how the network's output probability distribution changes under those perturbations. For annotation, SoQal dynamically chooses between requesting an oracle label and assigning a pseudo-label. Selection and expert questioning therefore become separate decisions within one framework.

The authors show that BALC can outperform acquisition functions such as BALD. They also report that SoQal outperforms baseline methods even when the oracle supplies noisy labels. These findings support considering the annotation decision alongside acquisition: identifying an informative example does not automatically determine that an expert must label it. The framework makes that additional choice explicit.
icml-2022-soqal-selective-oracle-questio.tldr: BALC selects examples through prediction consistency, while SoQal chooses whether each needs an expert label or a pseudo-label.

paragraphs: The hybrid model of differential privacy combines many local agents with a curator holding sensitive data from additional individuals. This paper studies learning when the curator's examples come from a different distribution than the local agents' population. The challenge is to use that mismatched dataset for private transfer learning.

The authors propose Subsample-Test-Reweigh, a general scheme that converts a curator-model learner into a hybrid-model learner. It repeatedly subsamples and reweights the curator's examples using a smooth variant of the multiplicative-weights algorithm. The scheme's sample complexity depends on the chi-squared divergence between the two distributions, making the distribution mismatch an explicit part of the data requirement.

The paper provides worst-case sample-complexity bounds for this private reduction. It also identifies two specific settings where the required sample count can decrease substantially, supporting one mathematically and the other empirically. The contribution is a general transfer mechanism with quantified data requirements, together with more favorable cases whose supporting evidence is explicitly distinguished.
icml-2022-transfer-learning-in-different.tldr: Subsample-Test-Reweigh enables private transfer learning in the hybrid model, with sample requirements tied to distribution mismatch.

paragraphs: Personalizing a deep-learning service usually requires additional training on a person's data. This paper proposes generating personalized model weights through forward computation instead. The aim is to make personalization possible on devices such as phones without installing a training platform or performing additional fine-tuning there.

The method uses a variational hyper-personalizer to capture a distribution over layer weights suited to the target person. It assumes that even one personal example can convey useful characteristics of that person. At test time, a small enrollment set passes through the hyper-personalizer, which estimates personalized weights on the fly. The personal examples therefore inform weight generation directly.

Experiments show that forwarding a handful of examples can produce reliable personalized models without back-propagating through those examples. The approach can also use a single enrollment example, under the motivating assumption that it carries relevant personal information. Its practical contribution is to move the personalization procedure from device-side fine-tuning to inference through an already learned weight-generating model.
icml-2022-variational-on-the-fly-persona.tldr: A variational hyper-personalizer generates personalized model weights from a few enrollment examples without device-side fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Vision transformers classify images effectively, but their complexity makes their decisions difficult to interpret. Attention maps offer visual clues, yet ambiguity in those maps can suggest incorrect relationships between image patches. This paper introduces ViT-NeT to make classification decisions easier to examine while improving fine-grained recognition.

A vision transformer first produces contextual representations of image patches. A neural tree decoder then uses those representations for classification. The tree structure and prototypes describe the decision process and provide visual interpretations. The architecture targets categories that can look similar to one another while also containing substantial variation within a category, a central difficulty in fine-grained recognition.

The authors compare ViT-NeT with state-of-the-art methods on widely used fine-grained visual categorization benchmarks. Their experiments show superior classification performance and interpretability in those comparisons. The results support combining a transformer backbone with an explicitly structured decoder as a way to improve both objectives together, addressing the practical tension between predictive performance and understandable decisions.
icml-2022-vit-net-interpretable-vision-t.tldr: ViT-NeT adds a prototype-based neural tree decoder to a vision transformer, improving fine-grained classification and interpretability in benchmarks.
